purpose: Sacrosidase is used to help people who cannot digest certain sugars, especially sucrose (table sugar), because their body does not make enough of the enzyme needed to break it down. This condition is called Congenital Sucrase-Isomaltase Deficiency, or CSID. Without this medicine, eating sugary foods can cause painful stomach symptoms like diarrhea and cramping.
how_it_works: Normally, your small intestine makes an enzyme called sucrase that breaks down sucrose (table sugar) into smaller sugars your body can absorb. If you have CSID, your body does not make enough of this enzyme, so sugar sits in your gut and causes problems. Sacrosidase is a liquid form of that missing enzyme — you take it with meals and it does the job your body cannot do on its own.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, difficulty sleeping, headache, and nervousness. Most side effects are mild and related to the digestive system.
warnings: This medicine is made from yeast, so it should NOT be used if you are allergic to yeast, yeast products, or papain (found in papaya). Serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, have been reported. Do not mix or take this medicine with fruit juice, as juice can destroy the enzyme and make it stop working. Always store it in the refrigerator and use it within 4 weeks of opening.
typical_dosing: The dose depends on your weight. For children and adults under about 33 pounds, the usual dose is 1 mL (about half a teaspoon) with each meal or snack. For those over 33 pounds, the usual dose is 2 mL (about 1 teaspoon) with each meal or snack. Your doctor will tell you exactly how much to take. Always take it with water or milk — never with juice.
